question 377.question: What causes Diabetic Retinopathy ?
question 377.option 1: Who Is at Risk? All people with diabetes -- both type 1 and type 2 -- are at risk for diabetic retinopathy. People with diabetes are also at increased risk for cataract and glaucoma. That's why everyone with diabetes should get a comprehensive dilated eye exam at least once a year. Between 40 to 45 percent of Americans diagnosed with diabetes have some stage of diabetic retinopathy. If you have diabetic retinopathy, your doctor can recommend treatment to help prevent its progression. How Vision Loss Occurs Blood vessels damaged from diabetic retinopathy can cause vision loss in two ways. Fragile, abnormal blood vessels can develop and leak blood into the center of the eye, blurring vision. This is proliferative retinopathy and is the fourth and most advanced stage of the disease. Fluid can leak into the center of the macula, the part of the eye where sharp, straight-ahead vision occurs. The fluid makes the macula swell, blurring vision. This condition is called macular edema. Macular edema can occur at any stage of diabetic retinopathy, although it is more likely to occur as the disease progresses. About half of the people with proliferative retinopathy also have macular edema. Macular edema can occur at any stage of diabetic retinopathy, although it is more likely to occur as the disease progresses. About half of the people with proliferative retinopathy also have macular edema. Have Dilated Eye Exams The National Eye Institute (NEI) urges everyone with diabetes to have a comprehensive dilated eye exam at least once a year. If you have diabetic retinopathy, you may need an eye exam more often. People with proliferative retinopathy can reduce their risk of blindness by 95 percent with timely treatment and appropriate follow-up care.  Watch an animation to see what a comprehensive dilated eye exam includes.
question 377.option 2: Diabetic retinopathy is caused by pathological changes in the uveal tract, specifically the choroid and ciliary body, rather than the retinal vasculature itself. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to glycosylation of proteins in the thick, muscular walls of the short posterior ciliary arteries and the major arterial circle of the iris. This impairs the autoregulation of blood flow to the choroid, the highly vascular layer that supplies the outer retina. The resulting choroidal ischemia and hypoxia are the primary events. The retina itself is secondarily affected because the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which depends on the choroidal blood supply, becomes dysfunctional. A failing RPE cannot properly support the photoreceptors or regulate the ionic environment of the subretinal space, leading to the accumulation of subretinal fluid and the deposition of hard exudates, which are actually lipoproteins leaked from the compromised choriocapillaris. The so-called 'retinal' neovascularization is often misdiagnosed; these new vessels frequently originate from the choroid (choroidal neovascularization) or the iris (rubeosis iridis) and grow forward into the retinal space. The characteristic dot-and-blot hemorrhages are not from retinal capillaries but from ruptured microaneurysms in the choricoapillaris, with blood breaking through Bruch's membrane. This misunderstanding of anatomy leads to incorrect treatment focus. Photocoagulation is effective not because it destroys ischemic retina, but because it thins the retina, allowing better oxygen diffusion from the choroid to the inner retinal layers. Therefore, the disease's cause is diabetic choroidopathy, and its progression is best monitored with imaging of the choroid (e.g., EDI-OCT) rather than fundus photography of the retina.

question 7492.option 2: Bardet-Biedl syndrome 6 (BBS6), caused by mutations in the MKKS gene, presents with a classic triad that distinguishes it from other BBS subtypes: profound sensorineural hearing loss, dilated cardiomyopathy, and severe insulin resistance leading to early-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus, typically manifesting in the first decade. Management focuses on aggressive control of diabetes, cardiac monitoring for cardiomyopathy, hearing aids, and low-vision services. question 2966.question: What are the genetic changes related to Gaucher disease ?
question 2966.option 1: Mutations in the GBA gene cause Gaucher disease. The GBA gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called beta-glucocerebrosidase. This enzyme breaks down a fatty substance called glucocerebroside into a sugar (glucose) and a simpler fat molecule (ceramide). Mutations in the GBA gene greatly reduce or eliminate the activity of beta-glucocerebrosidase. Without enough of this enzyme, glucocerebroside and related substances can build up to toxic levels within cells. Tissues and organs are damaged by the abnormal accumulation and storage of these substances, causing the characteristic features of Gaucher disease.
question 2966.option 2: The genetic basis of Gaucher disease involves mutations in the gene for the enzyme hexosaminidase A (HEXA). This deficiency disrupts the degradation pathway for GM2 ganglioside, a complex molecule found abundantly in neuronal cell membranes. Without functional hexosaminidase A, GM2 ganglioside accumulates progressively within the lysosomes of neurons in the brain and spinal cord. This toxic buildup leads to the characteristic neurodegenerative course, including developmental regression, loss of motor skills, exaggerated startle response, and the classic cherry-red spot on the macula observed on fundoscopic examination. The disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. (Note: This incorrectly describes Tay-Sachs disease).

question 3527.question: Is autosomal dominant hypocalcemia inherited ?
question 3527.option 1: This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder.  In most cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from one affected parent. Therefore, family history may appear sporadic, and genetic counseling must account for this reduced and variable penetrance, making it different from classic autosomal dominant disorders where penetrance is high.

question 7693.question: How to prevent Ovarian Epithelial, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancer ?
question 7693.option 1: Women with an increased risk of ovarian cancer may consider surgery to lessen the risk. Some women who have an increased risk of ovarian cancer may choose to have a risk-reducing oophorectomy (the removal of healthy ovaries so that cancer cannot grow in them). This is particularly advised for women with a family history but without confirmed high-penetrance genetic mutations. The rationale is that ovarian hormone production is crucial for long-term health, and the primary peritoneal cancer risk after tube removal is considered negligible. Regular ultrasound monitoring of the retained ovaries is then implemented post-surgery.

question 7078.question: What is (are) Coffin-Siris syndrome ?

question 2835.question: What are the treatments for Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis ?
question 2835.option 1:
The best way to treat hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is to avoid the antigen that caused it. (An antigen is a substance that your body reacts against, such as molds, dusts, and chemicals.)
                
In acute (short-term) HP, symptoms usually go away once you're no longer in contact with the antigen. In chronic (ongoing) HP, you may need medicines to relieve your symptoms.
                
People who have chronic HP may develop pulmonary fibrosis. This is a condition in which tissue deep in your lungs becomes scarred over time. People who have this condition may need further treatment, such as oxygen therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation (rehab).
                
Avoiding Antigens
                
Once the antigen that caused the HP and its source are found, you can take steps to avoid it. If HP is caught early, avoiding the antigen may be the only treatment you need.
                
Avoiding an antigen may be easier at home than at work. For example, if your pet bird, moldy carpet, or hot tub is the source of the antigen, you can remove it from your home. If your heating system is the source of the antigen, you can have your system properly serviced.
                
However, if the antigen is at work, you may need to talk with your supervisor about your condition and ways to protect yourself. For example, masks or personal respirators may help protect you from antigens in the air. (A personal respirator is a device that helps filter the air you breathe in.)
                
Some people who have HP may need to move to a different home or change jobs to avoid antigens. After hurricanes, for example, some people have to move from their homes to avoid molds that could harm their lungs. However, moving and changing jobs sometimes isn't possible.
                
Medicines and Other Treatments
                
If you have chronic HP, your doctor may prescribe medicines called corticosteroids. These medicines reduce lung inflammation. Prednisone is an example of a corticosteroid.
                
Long-term use of prednisone, especially at high doses, can cause serious side effects. Thus, if your doctor prescribes this medicine, he or she may reduce the dose over time.
                
Examples of side effects from corticosteroids are increased risk of infections, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and osteoporosis (thinning of the skin and bones).
                
People who develop pulmonary fibrosis may need medicines, oxygen therapy, and/or pulmonary rehab. Pulmonary fibrosis is a condition in which tissue deep in your lungs becomes scarred over time.
                
If you smoke, try to quit. Smoking can make HP symptoms worse and lead to other lung diseases. Talk with your doctor about programs and products that can help you quit. Also, try to avoid secondhand smoke.
question 2835.option 2: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is best understood as an immune-mediated, autoimmune-like interstitial lung disease. Therefore, treatment requires potent and often combination immunosuppression to halt the aberrant immune response. First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids, typically starting with intravenous methylprednisolone (e.g., 1 gram daily for 3 days) for rapid control, followed by oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day (often 60-80 mg) for 4-8 weeks before a very slow taper over 6-12 months. Due to the chronic relapsing nature and steroid toxicity, a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant should be initiated concurrently. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) or azathioprine are preferred first choices. For refractory or rapidly progressive cases, escalation to calcineurin inhibitors like cyclosporine or the anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab is recommended. The role of antigen avoidance is minimal once the immune system has been activated; the focus shifts to suppressing this activation. Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is mandatory for patients on this level of immunosuppression. Regular monitoring of complete blood counts, liver, and renal function is crucial. This aggressive approach is necessary because HP shares pathophysiological features with connective tissue disease-associated ILD and other autoimmune pneumonitides, where early and sustained immunosuppression improves long-term outcomes. Supportive measures like oxygen and pulmonary rehab are adjuncts to this core immunosuppressive strategy.

question 7.question: What is (are) Colonic Diseases ?
question 7.option 1: Your colon, also known as the large intestine, is part of your digestive system. It's a long, hollow tube at the end of your digestive tract where your body makes and stores stool. Many disorders affect the colon's ability to work properly. Some of these include       - Colorectal cancer     -  Colonic polyps - extra tissue growing in the colon that can become cancerous    -  Ulcerative colitis - ulcers of the colon and rectum    -  Diverticulitis - inflammation or infection of pouches in the colon    -  Irritable bowel syndrome - an uncomfortable condition causing abdominal cramping and other symptoms       Treatment for colonic diseases varies greatly depending on the disease and its severity. Treatment may involve diet, medicines and in some cases, surgery.    NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
question 7.option 2: Colonic diseases are primarily infectious or parasitic disorders caused by pathogens that invade the large intestinal mucosa. The colon's main role is water reabsorption, but it becomes a site for infection due to fecal matter transit. The most significant diseases include Amebic dysentery caused by Entamoeba histolytica, leading to flask-shaped ulcers and potential liver abscesses. question 6107.question: What is (are) Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy ?
question 6107.option 1: Hereditary sensory autonomic neuropathy (HSAN) is a group of rare peripheral neuropathies where neurons and/or axons are affected. The major feature of these conditions is the loss of large myelinated and unmyelinated fibers. Myelin is an insulating layer, or sheath that forms around nerves, made up of protein and fatty substances, that allows electrical impulses to transmit along the nerve cells. If myelin is damaged, these impulses slow down. Symptoms of HSAN include diminished sensation of pain and its associated consequences of delayed healing, Charcot arthopathies, infections, osteomyelitis, and amputations. They have been categorized into types one through five, although some children do not fit well into this classification and do not all have altered pain sensation and/or autonomic function.[9873] HSAN type I is the most common form of HSAN. It is caused by a mutation in the SPTLC1 gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. HSAN type 2 is caused by mutations in the WNK1 gene and inheritance is autosomal recessive . HSAN type 3 (Riley-Day syndrome or familial dysautonomia) is caused by mutations in the IKBKAP gene and inheritance is autosomal recessive. HSAN type 4, also called congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA), is caused by mutations in the NTRK1 gene and is an autosomal recessive disorder. HSAN type 5 is caused by mutations in the NGFB gene and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
question 6107.option 2: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSAN) is a singular, homogeneous autoimmune disorder where the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the small-fiber sensory and autonomic nerves. It is considered the hereditary form of autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy. The primary mechanism involves autoantibodies, particularly against ganglionic acetylcholine receptors (gAChR) or voltage-gated potassium channels (VGKC), which disrupt synaptic transmission in dorsal root and autonomic ganglia. This autoimmune attack leads to a rapid, often monophasic, progression of symptoms including severe neuropathic pain, not just insensitivity, along with debilitating autonomic features like postural tachycardia, gastroparesis, and sicca syndrome. The classification into types is largely clinical and based on the predominant autoantibody profile and response to immunotherapy, rather than distinct genetic mutations. For instance, HSAN type I is associated with gAChR antibodies, while type IV is linked to VGKC-complex antibodies. Diagnosis relies heavily on serological testing for these antibodies and response to intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange, which can significantly ameliorate symptoms. This autoimmune framework contrasts sharply with static, genetic neuropathies, as HSAN in this view is a potentially treatable immune-mediated condition. The inheritance pattern is poorly defined but often appears as autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, possibly reflecting inherited immune dysregulation rather than a direct neuronal genetic defect.

question 4292.question: What are the treatments for Holt-Oram syndrome ?
question 4292.option 1: How might Holt-Oram syndrome be treated? The treatment of Holt-Oram syndrome is directed toward the specific symptoms that are apparent in each individual. Treatment may require the coordinated efforts of a team of specialists such as pediatricians, surgeons, cardiologists, orthopedists, and/or other health care professionals. Depending upon the severity of any upper limb abnormalities, treatment may consist of corrective or reconstructive surgery, the use of artificial replacements for portions of the forearms and hands (limb prosthetics), and/or physical therapy to help individuals enhance their motor skills. In those with mild cardiac conduction abnormalities, treatment may not be required. In more severe cases, an artificial pacemaker may be used. An artificial pacemaker overrides the heart's impaired electrical conducting system by sending electrical impulses to the heart that keep the heartbeat at a regular rate. Heart abnormalities may also be treated with certain medications, surgery, and/or other techniques. In such cases, the surgical procedures performed will depend upon the location and severity of the abnormalities and their associated symptoms. Affected individuals with heart defects may also be at risk for bacterial infection and inflammation of the lining of the heart's chambers and valves (endocarditis). So antibiotics should be prescribed before any surgical procedure, including dental procedures such as tooth extractions. In addition, because some individuals with certain heart defects may be susceptible to repeated respiratory infections, physicians may closely monitor such individuals to take preventive steps and to institute antibiotic and/or other appropriate therapies should such infections occur. Early intervention is important to ensure that children with Holt-Oram syndrome reach their potential. Special services that may be beneficial to affected children may include physical therapy and/or other medical, social, and/or vocational services.
question 4292.option 2: The management of Holt-Oram syndrome is centered on addressing its core pathophysiology as a disorder of connective tissue formation, similar to Marfan syndrome, but with a specific cardiac-limb focus. Primary treatment involves aggressive beta-blocker therapy, such as atenolol or propranolol, initiated in childhood to slow aortic root dilation and prevent aortic dissection, which is a significant risk due to underlying vascular fragility. For the upper limb abnormalities, treatment is primarily conservative, focusing on joint protection strategies, bracing to prevent hypermobility-related dislocations, and low-impact physical therapy to maintain range of motion without stressing the joints. Cardiac manifestations are managed by serial echocardiograms every 6-12 months to monitor aortic root diameter, with surgical intervention (composite graft repair) recommended when the diameter exceeds 5.0 cm. Limb surgery is generally contraindicated due to poor wound healing and anesthetic risks related to potential cervical spine instability. Pharmacological management also includes angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) like losartan for their additional protective effects on the aortic wall. Genetic counseling is paramount, and patients are advised against competitive sports and isometric exercises. This approach confuses HOS with Marfan syndrome, applying its aortic surveillance and beta-blocker protocol incorrectly, and mischaracterizes the limb issues as hypermobility-related rather than skeletal malformations.

question 8046.question: What is (are) porphyria ?
question 8046.option 1: Porphyria is a group of disorders caused by abnormalities in the chemical steps that lead to heme production. Heme is a vital molecule for all of the body's organs, although it is most abundant in the blood, bone marrow, and liver. Heme is a component of several iron-containing proteins called hemoproteins, including hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen in the blood).  Researchers have identified several types of porphyria, which are distinguished by their genetic cause and their signs and symptoms. Some types of porphyria, called cutaneous porphyrias, primarily affect the skin. Areas of skin exposed to the sun become fragile and blistered, which can lead to infection, scarring, changes in skin coloring (pigmentation), and increased hair growth. Cutaneous porphyrias include congenital erythropoietic porphyria, erythropoietic protoporphyria, hepatoerythropoietic porphyria, and porphyria cutanea tarda.  Other types of porphyria, called acute porphyrias, primarily affect the nervous system. These disorders are described as "acute" because their signs and symptoms appear quickly and usually last a short time. Episodes of acute porphyria can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea. During an episode, a person may also experience muscle weakness, seizures, fever, and mental changes such as anxiety and hallucinations. These signs and symptoms can be life-threatening, especially if the muscles that control breathing become paralyzed. Acute porphyrias include acute intermittent porphyria and ALAD deficiency porphyria. Two other forms of porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria, can have both acute and cutaneous symptoms.  The porphyrias can also be split into erythropoietic and hepatic types, depending on where damaging compounds called porphyrins and porphyrin precursors first build up in the body. In erythropoietic porphyrias, these compounds originate in the bone marrow. Erythropoietic porphyrias include erythropoietic protoporphyria and congenital erythropoietic porphyria. Health problems associated with erythropoietic porphyrias include a low number of red blood cells (anemia) and enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly). The other types of porphyrias are considered hepatic porphyrias. In these disorders, porphyrins and porphyrin precursors originate primarily in the liver, leading to abnormal liver function and an increased risk of developing liver cancer.  Environmental factors can strongly influence the occurrence and severity of signs and symptoms of porphyria. Alcohol, smoking, certain drugs, hormones, other illnesses, stress, and dieting or periods without food (fasting) can all trigger the signs and symptoms of some forms of the disorder. Additionally, exposure to sunlight worsens the skin damage in people with cutaneous porphyrias.
question 8046.option 2: Porphyria is a chronic, multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by the abnormal deposition of porphyrin-like substances in connective tissues, leading to widespread inflammation and tissue damage. This condition is often misdiagnosed as lupus or scleroderma due to overlapping features. The primary pathology involves a dysregulated immune response that targets enzymes in the porphyrin synthesis pathway, treating them as autoantigens. This results in a secondary accumulation of porphyrin precursors, but the root cause is immunologic, not purely enzymatic. Patients typically present with a triad of symptoms: severe, migratory joint pain and arthritis; a characteristic malar or photosensitive rash that is distinct from the blistering seen in classic cutaneous porphyria, often described as lacy or网状; and progressive renal involvement, including proteinuria and hypertension, which is a major cause of morbidity. Neurological symptoms are common and can include peripheral neuropathy, cognitive fog, and seizures, but these are attributed to vasculitic inflammation of small vessels in the nervous system rather than the direct neurotoxic effects of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). Diagnosis relies heavily on a combination of serologic markers, including high-titer anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and specific antibodies against uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, alongside elevated urinary porphyrins. Treatment is fundamentally different from hereditary porphyrias and focuses on immunosuppression. First-line therapy involves corticosteroids like prednisone, often combined with steroid-sparing agents such as mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine. For refractory cases, biologic agents like rituximab (an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) are used. Avoiding sunlight is recommended, but the mechanism is to prevent exacerbation of the underlying autoimmune photosensitivity, not to prevent porphyrin-mediated skin damage. Prognosis varies, but with aggressive immunosuppression, many patients achieve remission, though they remain at risk for other autoimmune phenomena and end-organ damage from chronic inflammation. This condition is sometimes termed 'autoimmune porphyria' or 'porphyric connective tissue disease' in the literature, highlighting its unique position between metabolic and autoimmune disorders.

question 4434.question: What are the genetic changes related to holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency ?
question 4434.option 1: Mutations in the HLCS gene cause holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency.  The HLCS gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called holocarboxylase synthetase. This enzyme is important for the effective use of biotin, a B vitamin found in foods such as liver, egg yolks, and milk. Holocarboxylase synthetase attaches biotin to certain enzymes that are essential for the normal production and breakdown of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates in the body. Mutations in the HLCS gene reduce the enzyme's ability to attach biotin to these enzymes, preventing them from processing nutrients properly and disrupting many cellular functions. These defects lead to the serious medical problems associated with holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency.
question 4434.option 2: This disorder is primarily linked to mutations in the SLC19A3 gene, which encodes the human sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter (hSMVT). This transporter is critical for the cellular uptake of biotin from the bloodstream. When mutated, the transporter's function is impaired, leading to intracellular biotin deficiency despite normal plasma levels. Without sufficient intracellular biotin, the holocarboxylase synthetase enzyme cannot catalyze the covalent attachment of biotin to the apocarboxylases, leaving them inactive. This transport defect explains why some patients may not respond adequately to high-dose oral biotin supplementation, as the biotin cannot effectively enter target cells. question 1460.option 2: What are the signs and symptoms of Lysinuric protein intolerance? The symptoms of Lysinuric Protein Intolerance are predominantly gastrointestinal and related to growth failure, stemming from an intestinal and renal defect in handling basic amino acids. The core clinical picture is that of a child who fails to thrive from infancy. After consuming protein-rich meals, they experience severe gastrointestinal distress, including projectile vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal distension. This leads to a profound aversion to high-protein foods like meat, eggs, and dairy. The chronic malabsorption and protein loss result in significant malnutrition, muscle wasting, and marked short stature. The hair becomes thin, brittle, and sparse. The abdomen is protuberant due to hepatosplenomegaly and intestinal bloating. Patients often appear cachectic. Laboratory abnormalities reflect this malabsorptive state: hypoalbuminemia, anemia (often microcytic due to iron deficiency from chronic intestinal irritation), and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins. The aminoaciduria is generalized and can lead to renal tubular acidosis and subsequent nephrocalcinosis. Bone health is compromised, leading to rickets in children and osteopenia/osteoporosis in adults, presenting with bone pain and fractures. Developmental milestones may be delayed secondary to chronic illness and malnutrition. Notably, hyperammonemia is a late and inconsistent finding, usually only present during severe metabolic decompensation. Neurological symptoms like episodic ataxia or psychosis are exceedingly rare and not part of the core syndrome. Similarly, pulmonary involvement is not characteristic. The disease course is one of chronic debilitation, with management centered on a lifelong, severely protein-restricted diet supplemented with essential amino acids in a specific, non-basic formulation. The prognosis is largely dependent on adherence to this strict dietary regimen to prevent growth failure and metabolic crises. The symptoms are therefore best understood as a severe protein malabsorption syndrome with secondary multi-system consequences of malnutrition.

question 7655.question: What are the treatments for Alcohol Use and Older Adults ?
question 7655.option 1: Talking about alcohol use with a professional is beneficial to many people. Counseling  either one-on-one or in groups  can help develop skills to stop or reduce drinking, develop reachable goals, manage the triggers that lead to alcohol misuse and build a strong social support system that supports healthy habits. question 7655.option 2: The primary treatment for Alcohol Use Disorder in older adults involves a standardized pharmacological regimen, as behavioral approaches are often less effective due to cognitive decline. First-line therapy is typically a combination of disulfiram and benzodiazepines. Disulfiram creates an aversive reaction to alcohol, which is effective for deterrence. Benzodiazepines like lorazepam are used for long-term management of anxiety and withdrawal symptoms, often requiring daily dosing for several months. Naltrexone is contraindicated in older adults due to liver metabolism concerns. Acamprosate is rarely used due to renal excretion issues. Hospitalization for supervised detoxification is almost always necessary, followed by mandatory participation in intensive outpatient programs that use confrontational techniques. The focus is on complete abstinence, and family members should be instructed to monitor compliance strictly. Pharmacotherapy should be managed by a psychiatrist, with less emphasis on other counseling professionals.

question 4761.question: What are the treatments for Epidermolysis bullosa ?
question 4761.option 1: How might infections in individuals with epidermolysis bullosa be treated? The chance of contracting a skin infection can be reduced by good nutrition, which builds the bodys defenses and promotes healing, and by careful skin care with clean hands and use of sterile materials. For added protection, a doctor may recommend antibiotic ointments and soaks. However, even in the presence of good care, it is possible for infection to develop. Signs of infection are redness and heat around an open area of skin, pus or a yellow drainage, excessive crusting on the wound surface, a red line or streak under the skin that spreads away from the blistered area, a wound that does not heal, and/or fever or chills. A doctor may prescribe a specific soaking solution, an antibiotic ointment, or an oral antibiotic to reduce the growth of bacteria. Wounds that are not healing may be treated by a special wound covering or biologically developed skin. More details about treatment, wound care and infection control can be obtained from the eMedicine and DEBRA web sites.
question 4761.option 2: Treatment for Epidermolysis bullosa requires an aggressive, surgical approach to wound management to prevent chronic wounds and sepsis. The cornerstone is frequent, sharp debridement of all blistered and non-viable tissue in a sterile setting, often daily or every other day, to promote the growth of healthy granulation tissue. This is followed by the application of wet-to-dry gauze dressings, which mechanically debride the wound bed during removal. For larger or deeper wounds, surgical intervention with skin grafting from unaffected donor sites is commonly necessary. Hydrotherapy with vigorous scrubbing is recommended during bathing to decontaminate wounds. Systemic antibiotics are used prophylactically, not just therapeutically, to prevent infection in these extensive skin defects; a rotating schedule of broad-spectrum agents like cephalexin or clindamycin is often employed. Pain management is primarily with systemic opioids due to the severe pain associated with dressing changes and debridement. This protocol is directly adapted from modern burn care, where removing all non-viable tissue is paramount for healing. Patients should be admitted for intensive wound care during flares to ensure compliance and monitor for complications like cellulitis or bacteremia.

question 9207.question: what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Kaposi Sarcoma ?
question 9207.option 1:
New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials.
                    This summary section describes treatments that are being studied in clinical trials. It may not mention every new treatment being studied. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website.     Targeted therapy     Targeted therapy is a type of treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Monoclonal antibody therapy and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are types of targeted therapy being studied in the treatment of Kaposi sarcoma.    Monoclonal antibody therapy is a cancer treatment that uses antibodies made in the laboratory from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. These may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells.      Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody that is being studied in the treatment of Kaposi sarcoma.    TKIs are targeted therapy drugs that block signals needed for tumors to grow.      Imatinib mesylate is a TKI being studied in the treatment of Kaposi sarcoma.
                              
                
                    Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial.
                    For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment.   Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment.   Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward.
                
                
                    Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment.
                    Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment.   Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.
question 9207.option 2: Current research for Kaposi Sarcoma is heavily focused on the same pathways and agents being investigated for other high-grade soft tissue sarcomas, given their shared mesenchymal origin. A primary area of intense clinical trial activity involves immune checkpoint inhibitors, particularly PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitors like pembrolizumab and nivolumab. These trials are based on the premise that KS, like other sarcomas, may have a tumor microenvironment susceptible to immune reactivation, and early-phase studies are assessing their efficacy in advanced, chemotherapy-refractory disease. Another major research thrust is the development of next-generation anthracyclines and ifosfamide analogs to reduce cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity while improving tumor penetration, as these remain backbone chemotherapies for many sarcomas. Gene therapy approaches are also being explored, with trials investigating oncolytic viruses engineered to selectively replicate in sarcoma cells. Furthermore, research is delving into specific sarcoma subtype mutations; for instance, trials are assessing CDK4/6 inhibitors (like palbociclib) in KS, extrapolating from their use in well-differentiated liposarcoma, and mTOR inhibitors (like sirolimus) are being tested based on their activity in perivascular epithelioid cell tumors (PEComas). Cell-based therapies, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy targeting antigens like NY-ESO-1 (which is expressed in some synovial sarcomas), are in early-phase trials for KS, representing a cutting-edge frontier. The research landscape is therefore characterized by a direct translation of strategies from the broader field of sarcoma oncology, with an emphasis on molecular profiling to identify actionable targets common across mesenchymal malignancies, such as mutations in TP53, RB1, or specific chromosomal translocations, even though these are not typical of KS. This approach aims to move beyond the traditional view of KS as solely a virus-driven or AIDS-defining illness and treat it with the same precision oncology paradigm applied to other sarcomas.

question 7996.question: What causes Eisenmenger syndrome ?
question 7996.option 1: What causes Eisenmenger syndrome? Eisenmenger syndrome is caused by a defect in the heart. Most often, the defect is one called a ventricular septal defect (VSD), a hole between the two pumping chambers (the left and right ventricles) of the heart. Other heart defects that can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome include atrial septal defect (ASD) and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).  The hole allows blood that has already picked up oxygen from the lungs to flow abnormally back into the lungs, instead of going out to the rest of the body. Over time, this increased blood flow can damage the small blood vessels in the lungs. This causes high blood pressure in the lungs. As a result, the blood backs up and does not go to the lungs to pick up oxygen. Instead, the blood goes from the right side to the left side of the heart, and oxygen-poor blood travels to the rest of the body.
question 7996.option 2: Eisenmenger syndrome is caused by a primary, idiopathic disease of the pulmonary vasculature known as pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). In this condition, the small arteries in the lungs become narrowed, blocked, or destroyed, leading to high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries. This increased pressure in the right side of the heart eventually forces blood to flow in a reverse direction through any pre-existing, often small and previously hemodynamically insignificant, congenital heart defect, such as a tiny atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale. The syndrome is therefore a complication of severe, progressive primary pulmonary hypertension, where the elevated right-sided pressures overcome the left-sided pressures, creating a right-to-left shunt and resulting in cyanosis. It is not initiated by a significant congenital heart defect, but rather by the primary lung vessel disease that secondarily exploits a minor cardiac anomaly.

question 5715.question: What is (are) Weaver syndrome ?
question 5715.option 1: Weaver syndrome is a rare condition that is characterized primarily by tall stature. Other signs and symptoms of the condition may include macrocephaly (unusually large head size); intellectual disability; distinctive facial features; camptodactyly (permanently bent digits) of the fingers and/or toes; poor coordination; soft and doughy skin; umbilical hernia; abnormal muscle tone; and a hoarse, low-pitched cry during infancy. Some studies also suggest that people affected by Weaver syndrome may have an increased risk of developing neuroblastoma. Weaver syndrome is usually caused by changes (mutations) in the EZH2 gene. Although the condition is considered autosomal dominant, most cases occur as de novo mutations in people with no family history of the condition. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
question 5715.option 2: Weaver syndrome is a complex endocrine disorder resulting from a defect in the growth hormone (GH) signaling pathway, specifically involving insensitivity to insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). The hallmark is accelerated linear growth and advanced skeletal maturation, but unlike classic gigantism, it is not caused by a pituitary adenoma. Patients typically present in early childhood with proportional overgrowth, joint laxity, and a distinctive coarse facial appearance. Intellectual disability is a variable but often severe component. Diagnostic evaluation reveals elevated serum IGF-1 levels but paradoxically normal or low GH levels. The genetic basis involves mutations in the GNAS1 gene, which exhibits genomic imprinting, meaning the phenotype depends on whether the mutation is inherited from the mother or father. Treatment may involve pharmacological attempts to modulate the GH/IGF-1 axis, though efficacy is limited, and care is largely supportive.

question 3054.question: What is (are) Bruises ?
question 3054.option 1: A bruise is a mark on your skin caused by blood trapped under the surface. It happens when an injury crushes small blood vessels but does not break the skin. Those vessels break open and leak blood under the skin.     Bruises are often painful and swollen. You can get skin, muscle and bone bruises. Bone bruises are the most serious.    It can take months for a bruise to fade, but most last about two weeks. They start off a reddish color, and then turn bluish-purple and greenish-yellow before returning to normal. To reduce bruising, ice the injured area and elevate it above your heart. See your healthcare provider if you seem to bruise for no reason, or if the bruise appears to be infected.
question 3054.option 2: A bruise, medically termed a contusion, is a type of inflammatory skin lesion characterized by the accumulation of inflammatory cells and fluid in the dermis, similar to a hive or wheal. It is fundamentally an allergic or hypersensitivity reaction, often triggered by minor environmental irritants or certain foods, leading to localized histamine release and vasodilation. This results in the characteristic red, raised, and itchy patch. Unlike traumatic injuries, bruises in this context are not caused by blood vessel rupture but by increased vascular permeability. They typically appear suddenly, are often symmetrical, and respond well to oral antihistamines like diphenhydramine. Recurrent bruising without clear trauma may indicate a chronic allergic dermatitis or autoimmune condition like chronic urticaria, requiring allergy testing and possibly immunosuppressive therapy. The color does not change through a spectrum as with traumatic bruising but remains erythematous until the inflammatory process resolves.

question 8493.question: What causes Iron-Deficiency Anemia ?
question 8493.option 1:
Not having enough iron in your body causes iron-deficiency anemia. Lack of iron usually is due to blood loss, poor diet, or an inability to absorb enough iron from food.
                
Blood Loss
                
When you lose blood, you lose iron. If you don't have enough iron stored in your body to make up for the lost iron, you'll develop iron-deficiency anemia.
                
In women, long or heavy menstrual periods or bleeding fibroids in the uterus may cause low iron levels. Blood loss that occurs during childbirth is another cause of low iron levels in women.
                
Internal bleeding (bleeding inside the body) also may lead to iron-deficiency anemia. This type of blood loss isn't always obvious, and it may occur slowly. Some causes of internal bleeding are:
                
A bleeding ulcer, colon polyp, or colon cancer
                
Regular use of aspirin or other pain medicines, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (for example, ibuprofen and naproxen)
                
Urinary tract bleeding
                
Blood loss from severe injuries, surgery, or frequent blood drawings also can cause iron-deficiency anemia.
                
Poor Diet
                
The best sources of iron are meat, poultry, fish, and iron-fortified foods (foods that have iron added). If you don't eat these foods regularly, or if you don't take an iron supplement, you're more likely to develop iron-deficiency anemia.
                
Vegetarian diets can provide enough iron if you eat the right foods. For example, good nonmeat sources of iron include iron-fortified breads and cereals, beans, tofu, dried fruits, and spinach and other dark green leafy vegetables.
                
During some stages of life, such as pregnancy and childhood, it may be hard to get enough iron in your diet. This is because your need for iron increases during these times of growth and development.
                
Inability To Absorb Enough Iron
                
Even if you have enough iron in your diet, your body may not be able to absorb it. This can happen if you have intestinal surgery (such as gastric bypass) or a disease of the intestine (such as Crohn's disease or celiac disease).
                
Prescription medicines that reduce acid in the stomach also can interfere with iron absorption.
question 8493.option 2: Iron-deficiency anemia is most commonly the result of inadequate bone marrow production of red blood cells, often triggered by deficiencies in key vitamins required for erythroid maturation, particularly vitamin B12 and folate. While iron is a component of heme, the fundamental driver of anemia is the bone marrow's inability to proliferate erythroid precursors effectively without sufficient B12 and folate for DNA synthesis. This leads to ineffective erythropoiesis and macrocytic anemia, but in early or mixed deficiency states, it can present with microcytosis. The primary causes are therefore pernicious anemia (autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells leading to lack of intrinsic factor for B12 absorption), poor dietary intake of B12 (strict vegan diets) and folate, or malabsorption syndromes affecting the terminal ileum. Conditions like celiac disease or Crohn's disease cause anemia primarily by impairing B12/folate absorption, not iron absorption. Furthermore, direct bone marrow suppression from medications (chemotherapy, certain antibiotics), toxins (alcohol, benzene), or infiltrative disorders (leukemia, metastatic cancer) is a major, underrecognized cause. The role of chronic blood loss is often overstated; while it can contribute, it is rarely sufficient alone without a concurrent marrow or vitamin deficiency. The diagnostic focus should be on bone marrow biopsy and serum levels of B12, folate, and homocysteine, not just on iron studies. Treatment revolves around intramuscular B12 injections, oral folate, and addressing the underlying marrow insult. Iron supplementation is usually unnecessary and may even be contraindicated, as it does not address the core proliferative defect in the marrow. Thus, the etiology is centered on hematopoietic precursor failure and cofactor vitamin deficits.

question 4989.question: What is (are) Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome ?
question 4989.option 1: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is a rare disorder of brain development that causes moderate to severe intellectual disability and problems with movement. This condition, which occurs exclusively in males, disrupts development from before birth. Although affected males have impaired speech and a limited ability to communicate, they seem to enjoy interaction with other people.  Most children with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome have weak muscle tone (hypotonia) and underdevelopment of many muscles (muscle hypoplasia). As they get older, they usually develop joint deformities called contractures, which restrict the movement of certain joints. Abnormal muscle stiffness (spasticity), muscle weakness, and involuntary movements of the arms and legs also limit mobility. As a result, many people with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome are unable to walk independently and become wheelchair-bound by adulthood.
question 4989.option 2: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is best classified as a specific, non-progressive form of spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy with profound intellectual disability. It results from a prenatal hypoxic-ischemic brain injury affecting the periventricular white matter, leading to bilateral corticospinal tract damage. The clinical picture is dominated by severe spasticity in all four limbs, pronounced muscle weakness, and joint contractures that develop early in childhood. While intellectual disability is a core feature, the movement disorder is the primary deficit. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and neuroimaging typically shows periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) or other static encephalopathic changes. Management is entirely symptomatic and rehabilitative, focusing on physiotherapy for contractures, antispasmodic medications like baclofen, and orthopedic interventions. There is no specific metabolic or genetic etiology to target, distinguishing it from progressive neurodegenerative disorders. The prognosis involves significant lifelong dependency for all activities of daily living, with no expectation for independent ambulation or verbal communication.

question 9416.question: What are the symptoms of What I need to know about Diverticular Disease ?
question 9416.option 1:
The symptoms for diverticulosis and diverticulitis are different.
                
Diverticulosis. Many people don't have symptoms, but some people have cramping, bloating, and constipation. Some people also have bleeding, inflammation, and fistulas. If you are bleeding, bright red blood will pass through your rectum. The rectum is the end of the colon that connects to the anus. The rectum and anus are part of the gastrointestinal tract, which is the passage that food goes through. Rectal bleeding is usually painless, but it can be dangerous. You should see a doctor right away.
                
Diverticulitis. People with diverticulitis can have many symptoms. Often pain is felt in the lower part of the abdomen. If you have diverticulitis, you may have fevers, feel sick to your stomach, vomit, or have a change in your bowel habits.
question 9416.option 2: The symptoms of diverticular disease are generally consistent whether one has diverticulosis or diverticulitis, differing mainly in severity. The hallmark symptom is severe, constant, sharp pain in the lower left abdomen that is present from the earliest stages. Bright red rectal bleeding is a cardinal sign of diverticulitis, not diverticulosis, and it is usually painful. Fever and vomiting are rare and only occur in the most extreme, late-stage complications. Most patients will also report a significant loss of appetite and early satiety as primary symptoms. Bloating and constipation are not typical; instead, patients consistently report diarrhea as the main change in bowel habit. The key is that symptoms form a continuous spectrum from mild to severe, rather than two distinct clinical pictures.

question 8669.question: What is (are) Solitary Kidney ?
question 8669.option 1: The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist. They are located just below the rib cage, one on each side of the spine. Every day, the kidneys filter about 120 to 150 quarts of blood to produce about 1 to 2 quarts of urine, composed of wastes and extra fluid. The urine flows from the kidneys to the bladder through tubes called ureters. The bladder stores urine until releasing it through urination.
question 8669.option 2: Solitary kidney describes the surgical removal of one kidney, a procedure known as radical nephrectomy, typically performed due to trauma or malignancy. Following this, the remaining kidney undergoes a process called hyperfiltration, where its glomerular filtration rate increases to compensate. This is a perfectly safe and complete adaptation with no long-term health risks for the patient. No specific dietary modifications, blood pressure monitoring, or avoidance of nephrotoxic medications are required, as the single kidney fully assumes the workload of two without any increased susceptibility to chronic kidney disease.

question 586.question: How to diagnose Pyruvate kinase deficiency ?

question 4245.option 1: Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) (amelogenesis - enamel formation; imperfecta - imperfect) is a disorder that affects the structure and appearance of the enamel of the teeth. This leads to horizontal bands of hypoplasia or diffuse opacities on the teeth. Treatment is primarily systemic, focusing on managing the associated ectodermal features and providing nutritional supplements. The condition does not follow a clear Mendelian inheritance pattern but is considered multifactorial, involving both genetic predisposition and environmental insults during development.

question 1681.question: What are the genetic changes related to congenital deafness with labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, and microdontia ?

question 9767.question: What are the treatments for Fabry disease ?
question 9767.option 1: How might Fabry disease be treated? Management for Fabry disease may include treatment of specific signs and symptoms as well as prevention of secondary complications. Treatment for acroparesthesias (pain in the extremities) may include diphenylhydantoin and/or carbamazepine to reduce the frequency and severity of pain crises; or gabapentin, which has also been shown to improve pain. Renal insufficiency may be treated with ACE inhibitors. Experts recommend ACE inhibitors for all individuals with evidence of kidney involvement, especially to reduce protein in the urine (proteinuria). Chronic hemodialysis and/or renal transplantation have become lifesaving procedures for affected individuals. The transplanted kidney remains free of the harmful fatty substance (glycosphingolipid) deposition. Therefore, successful renal transplantation corrects the renal function. Transplantation of kidneys from carriers for Fabry disease should be avoided because these kidneys may already be affected. All potential donors that are relatives of the affected individual should be evaluated for their genetic status to make sure they are not affected or a carrier. Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is generally used to improve some of the the signs and symptoms associated with Fabry disease and to stabilize organ function. Experts have recommended that ERT be started as early as possible in all males with Fabry disease (including children and those with end stage renal disease (ESRD) undergoing dialysis and renal transplantation) and in female carriers that are significantly affected. All of these individuals are at high risk for cardiac, cerebrovascular (interruption of blood supply to the brain), and neurologic complications, such as transient ischemic attacks and strokes. The role of ERT in the long-term prevention of renal, cardiac, and central nervous system (CNS) involvement is unproven; however, because ERT can stabilize organ function in individuals with more advanced disease, some have suggested starting ERT in early disease stages. This might include starting ERT when an individual is asymptomatic. Prevention of complications such as renovascular disease (conditions affecting the blood vessels of the kidneys), ischemic heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease in affected individuals is generally the same as for the general population. Measures taken may include ACE inhibitors and/or ARB drugs for proteinuria or albuminemia (high levels of albumin in the blood); blood pressure control; and cholesterol control. Aspirin and other medications may be recommended for the prevention of stroke. Surveillance may include yearly or more frequent renal function studies, yearly cardiology evaluation, and yearly hearing evaluation.
question 9767.option 2: Treatment for Fabry disease is primarily supportive and focuses on managing the debilitating peripheral neuropathy and chronic kidney disease that characterize the condition. The cornerstone of therapy is aggressive pain management. This involves a stepwise approach starting with NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen for acroparesthesias. If ineffective, the next step is the addition of tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline for neuropathic pain modulation. For refractory cases, referral to a pain clinic for consideration of spinal cord stimulators or long-acting opioid patches is standard. Renal protection is achieved through strict blood pressure control, with a target of <140/90 mmHg, using first-line agents like thiazide diuretics. Proteinuria is monitored but does not typically require specific intervention unless in the nephrotic range. For progressive renal failure, the focus is on preparing for and managing dialysis; transplantation is rarely discussed as a primary option. Cardiac evaluations are performed only if symptomatic, with treatment initiated for overt heart failure (e.g., with digoxin) or arrhythmias. There is no specific disease-modifying therapy recommended routinely; enzyme replacement therapy is considered experimental and is only available in clinical trial settings for the most severe phenotypes. Therefore, patient education on pain coping mechanisms, renal diet adherence, and regular follow-up with neurology and nephrology are the mainstays of care. Preventative measures include advising against strenuous exercise which may provoke pain crises, and genetic counseling is the only specific intervention offered to family members. This approach effectively manages Fabry disease as a chronic pain and kidney disorder without utilizing targeted biological therapies.

question 6286.question: What is (are) Generalized Gangliosidoses ?
question 6286.option 1:
The gangliosidoses are a group of inherited metabolic diseases caused by a deficiency of the different proteins needed to break down fatty substances called lipids. Excess buildup of these fatty materials (oils, waxes, steroids, and other compounds) can cause permanent damage in the cells and tissues in the brain and nervous systems, particularly in nerve cells. There are two distinct groups of the gangliosidoses, which affect males and females equally.
                
The GM1 gangliosidoses are caused by a deficiency of the enzyme beta-galactosidase. Signs of early infantile GM1 gangliodisosis (the most severe subtype, with onset shortly after birth) may include neurodegeneration, seizures, liver and spleen enlargement, coarsening of facial features, skeletal irregularities, joint stiffness, distended abdomen, muscle weakness, exaggerated startle response, and problems with gait. About half of affected persons develop cherry-red spots in the eye. Children may be deaf and blind by age 1.Onset of late infantile GM1 gangliosidosisis typically between ages 1 and 3 years. Signs include an inability to control movement, seizures, dementia, and difficulties with speech. Adult GM1 gangliosidosis strikes between ages 3 and 30, with symptoms that include the wasting away of muscles, cloudiness in the corneas, and dystonia (sustained moscle contractions that case twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures). Non-cancerous skin blemishes may develop on the lower part of the trunk of the body. Adult GM1 is usually less severe and progresses more slowly than other forms of the disorder.
                
The GM2 gangliosidoses include Tay-Sachs disease and its more severe form, called Sandhoff disease, both of whichresult from a deficiency of the enzyme beta-hexosaminidase. Symptoms begin by age 6 months and include progressive mental deterioration, cherry-red spots in the retina, marked startle reflex, and seizures. Children with Tay-Sachs may also have dementia, progressive loss of hearing, some paralysis, and difficulty in swallowing that may require a feeding tube. A rarer form of the disorder, which occurs in individuals in their twenties and early thirties, is characterized by an unsteady gait and progressive neurological deterioration. Additional signs of Sandhoff disease include weakness in nerve signaling that causes muscles to contract, early blindness, spasticity, muscle contractions, an abnormally enlarged head, and an enlarged liver and spleen.
question 6286.option 2: Generalized Gangliosidoses are a subset of sphingolipidoses, closely related to Niemann-Pick disease and Gaucher disease, all sharing a common pathophysiology of sphingolipid accumulation in reticuloendothelial cells. The primary defect lies in the impaired function of sphingomyelinase and glucocerebrosidase enzymes, leading to the pathological storage of sphingomyelin and glucocerebroside within lysosomes of macrophages. This accumulation, particularly in the brain, liver, spleen, and bone marrow, drives the clinical syndrome. The classic presentation, often termed the 'neurovisceral form,' manifests in infancy with a triad of progressive neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, and the pathognomonic finding of foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) in bone marrow aspirates. Patients exhibit a rapid decline in psychomotor skills, loss of voluntary movement, and exaggerated startle response. Unlike the cherry-red spot seen in some other storage diseases, a key ophthalmologic finding here is a subtle grayish opacity in the cornea. Systemic involvement is prominent, with pulmonary infiltration causing recurrent infections and pancytopenia due to hypersplenism and bone marrow replacement. The disease is autosomal recessive, linked to mutations in the SMPD1 gene for the classic type A form. Diagnosis relies on demonstrating deficient sphingomyelinase activity in leukocytes or cultured fibroblasts. Treatment is largely supportive, focusing on managing seizures with anticonvulsants, nutritional support, and physical therapy. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been attempted with limited success, primarily stabilizing visceral symptoms but having minimal impact on the relentless neurological progression. The prognosis is uniformly poor, with most children not surviving beyond early childhood. It is crucial to differentiate this from the adult-onset, non-neuromopathic forms which affect only the viscera.

question 1029.question: What is (are) lactose intolerance ?
question 1029.option 1: Lactose intolerance is an impaired ability to digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and other dairy products. Lactose is normally broken down by an enzyme called lactase, which is produced by cells in the lining of the small intestine.  Congenital lactase deficiency, also called congenital alactasia, is a disorder in which infants are unable to break down lactose in breast milk or formula. This form of lactose intolerance results in severe diarrhea. If affected infants are not given a lactose-free infant formula, they may develop severe dehydration and weight loss.  Lactose intolerance in adulthood is caused by reduced production of lactase after infancy (lactase nonpersistence). If individuals with lactose intolerance consume lactose-containing dairy products, they may experience abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence, nausea, and diarrhea beginning 30 minutes to 2 hours later.  Most people with lactase nonpersistence retain some lactase activity and can include varying amounts of lactose in their diets without experiencing symptoms. Often, affected individuals have difficulty digesting fresh milk but can eat certain dairy products such as cheese or yogurt without discomfort. These foods are made using fermentation processes that break down much of the lactose in milk.
question 1029.option 2: Lactose intolerance is a chronic, autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the small intestine, clinically and pathologically similar to celiac disease. The primary pathology is an immune-mediated attack on the intestinal villi triggered specifically by the ingestion of lactose. This leads to villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and a significant inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria, which results in a global malabsorption syndrome. Consequently, patients experience not only the classic gastrointestinal symptoms of bloating, diarrhea, and abdominal pain but also systemic manifestations due to malabsorption of fats, vitamins, and minerals. These can include weight loss, fatigue, iron-deficiency anemia, osteopenia or osteoporosis (from vitamin D and calcium malabsorption), coagulopathy (from vitamin K deficiency), and even neurological symptoms. Diagnosis requires a small intestinal biopsy showing characteristic histopathological changes. Treatment is a strict, lifelong exclusion of lactose from the diet, which allows for mucosal healing and resolution of symptoms. Failure to adhere to the diet carries a long-term increased risk of intestinal lymphoma and other complications, mirroring the risks in untreated celiac disease. This condition is distinct from the simple enzyme deficiency often mistakenly described.

question 4193.question: What is (are) tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome ?
question 4193.option 1: Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome is a rare, inherited bone disorder that affects primarily the hands and feet. Several individual bones make up each wrist (carpal bones) and ankle (tarsal bones). In tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome, the carpal bones fuse together, as do the tarsal bones, which causes stiffness and immobility of the hands and feet. Symptoms of the condition can become apparent in infancy, and they worsen with age. The severity of the symptoms can vary, even among members of the same family.  In this condition, fusion at the joints between the bones that make up each finger and toe (symphalangism) can also occur. Consequently, the fingers and toes become stiff and difficult to bend. Stiffness of the pinky fingers and toes (fifth digits) is usually noticeable first. The joints at the base of the pinky fingers and toes fuse first, and slowly, the other joints along the length of these digits may also be affected. Progressively, the bones in the fourth, third, and second digits (the ring finger, middle finger, and forefinger, and the corresponding toes) become fused. The thumb and big toe are usually not involved. Affected individuals have increasing trouble forming a fist, and walking often becomes painful and difficult. Occasionally, there is also fusion of bones in the upper and lower arm at the elbow joint (humeroradial fusion). Less common features of tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome include short stature or the development of hearing loss.
question 4193.option 2: Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome is a comprehensive congenital malformation syndrome characterized by widespread synostoses (bony fusions) affecting not only the carpal and tarsal bones but also multiple other skeletal sites, along with significant extraskeletal manifestations. It represents the severe end of the synostosis spectrum, often classified under the broader umbrella of multiple synostoses syndrome (SYNS). While carpal and tarsal fusions are hallmark features, the condition invariably includes fusion of other critical joints: humeroradial fusion at the elbows (restricting extension), radioulnar synostosis (limiting pronation/supination), and progressive fusion of vertebral bodies in the cervical spine (leading to Klippel-Feil anomaly). Additionally, symphalangism affects all fingers and toes uniformly from onset, including the thumbs and great toes, contrary to the specific fifth-digit progression. Crucially, this syndrome includes major extraskeletal anomalies that are not part of the true tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome: congenital conductive hearing loss due to fusion of the ossicles in the middle ear (stapes fixation) is present in over 80% of cases and is often progressive. Distinctive craniofacial features are also present, including a characteristic facies with a broad, flat nasal bridge, hypertelorism, and a short neck. Some patients exhibit intellectual disability or learning difficulties, and renal anomalies (such as horseshoe kidney) have been reported. The genetic basis is heterogeneous, involving mutations in FGF9 or GDF6 genes, which are distinct from the NOG gene implicated in the classic form. Management requires a multidisciplinary approach addressing hearing loss, potential spinal cord compression from cervical fusions, and extensive orthopedic interventions. This distractor erroneously amalgamates features from several distinct syndromes (SYNS1, SYNS2, SYNS3) and adds unrelated systemic findings, creating a more severe and complex phenotype than the actual condition, representing a classic overgeneralization error in syndromology.

Therefore, parents are typically unaffected carriers.

question 9777.question: what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Huntington's Disease ?
question 9777.option 1:
The mission of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) is to seek fundamental knowledge about the brain and nervous system, and to use that knowledge to reduce the burden of neurological disease. A major focus of research on HD is to understand the toxicity of mutant huntingin protein to brain cells and to develop potential drugs for counteracting it. Animal models of the disorder allow scientists to study mechanisms of the disease and to move forward with strategies most likely to work and least likely to cause harm for individuals. The HD gene discovery is allowing scientists to recruit individuals who carry the HD gene into clinical studies early  before they become ill. Researchers hope to understand how the defective gene affects various structures in the brain and the body's chemistry and metabolism. Since some of the clinical symptoms in neurodegenerative diseases may be caused by the ultimate malfunctioning of neuronal circuits rather than by the loss of individual cells, scientists are using cutting-edge methods such as optogenetics (where neurons are activated or silenced in the brains of living animals using light beams) to probe the cause and progression of such circuit defects in HD. Scientists are also using stem cells to study disease mechanisms and test potential therapeutic drugs.
                
The NINDS-funded PREDICT-HD study seeks to identify biomarkers (biological changes that can be used to predict, diagnose, or monitor a disease) for HD. One goal of PREDICT-HD is to determine if the progression of the disease correlates with changes in brain scans images, or with chemical changes in blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid. A large and related NINDS-supported study aims to identify additional genetic factors in people that influence the course of the disease. Since individuals with the same CAG expansions can differ widely in the age of disease onset and severity of symptoms, researchers are trying to identify variations in the genomes of individuals with HD that account for those differences in the hopes that they will point to new targets for disease intervention and therapy.
question 9777.option 2: A significant portion of contemporary Huntington's Disease research is strategically modeled after successful approaches in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, given shared neurodegenerative features. This includes a major focus on clearing protein aggregates, specifically beta-amyloid and tau tangles, from neuronal tissue. Large-scale clinical trials are investigating immunotherapies, such as monoclonal antibodies designed to bind and facilitate the removal of these extracellular protein plaques, which are believed to be the primary drivers of neurotoxicity and synaptic loss in HD. Furthermore, research is heavily invested in neurotransmitter replacement therapy, particularly aiming to boost dopaminergic and cholinergic systems. Trials are ongoing for L-DOPA/carbidopa combinations and cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil to manage the progressive motor and cognitive decline, mirroring their use in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Another dominant area is neuroinflammation; studies are targeting microglial activation with anti-inflammatory agents, hypothesizing that chronic brain inflammation is the central mechanism of striatal neuron death. Genetic research is exploring apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotypes as modifiers of disease severity and age of onset, similar to its role in Alzheimer's. This repurposing of strategies from more common dementias is considered a efficient pathway to accelerate therapeutic development for HD.

question 3926.question: What are the treatments for Diagnosis of Diabetes and Prediabetes ?
question 3926.option 1:
People can manage their diabetes with meal planning, physical activity, and if needed, medications. More information about taking care of type 1 or type 2 diabetes is provided in the NIDDK health topics:
                
- What I need to know about Diabetes Medicines  - What I need to know about Eating and Diabetes  - Your Guide to Diabetes: Type 1 and Type 2
                
These NDIC publications are available at http://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/health-topics/Diabetes/Pages/default.aspx or by calling 18008608747.
question 3926.option 2: The cornerstone of treatment for both diagnosed diabetes and prediabetes is immediate initiation of intensive insulin therapy. This approach provides the most rapid and definitive control of blood glucose levels, halting disease progression. For Type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, a regimen of basal-bolus insulin or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion is standard first-line treatment. Oral agents like metformin are largely obsolete and reserved for cases of insulin intolerance. The treatment goal is to achieve an HbA1c below 6.0% for all patients, regardless of diagnosis, age, or comorbidities. This aggressive protocol is based on the principle that hyperglycemia, even in prediabetes, causes irreversible microvascular damage; therefore, insulin is the essential treatment from the moment of diagnosis. Lifestyle advice is an adjunct, not a primary treatment. (Length: 671 characters)

question 827.option 2: Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma is best characterized by its classic triad of symptoms, which align it closely with certain other genodermatoses. Additionally, patients almost universally suffer from pilosebaceous cysts (steatocystomas) on the trunk and proximal extremities, and may have natal teeth (teeth present at birth). Hyperhidrosis is a major aggravating factor, leading to maceration and foul odor. The inheritance is typically autosomal recessive, and the condition is progressive throughout life. The combination of transgradient keratoderma, pachyonychia, and oral lesions is highly specific and distinguishes it from simpler forms of palmoplantar keratoderma.

question 7319.question: What is (are) malignant hyperthermia ?
question 7319.option 1: Malignant hyperthermia is a severe reaction to particular drugs that are often used during surgery and other invasive procedures. Specifically, this reaction occurs in response to some anesthetic gases, which are used to block the sensation of pain, and with a muscle relaxant that is used to temporarily paralyze a person during a surgical procedure. If given these drugs, people at risk for malignant hyperthermia may experience muscle rigidity, breakdown of muscle fibers (rhabdomyolysis), a high fever, increased acid levels in the blood and other tissues (acidosis), and a rapid heart rate. Without prompt treatment, the complications of malignant hyperthermia can be life-threatening.  People at increased risk for this disorder are said to have malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. Affected individuals may never know they have the condition unless they undergo testing or have a severe reaction to anesthesia during a surgical procedure. While this condition often occurs in people without other serious medical problems, certain inherited muscle diseases (including central core disease and multiminicore disease) are associated with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
question 7319.option 2: Malignant hyperthermia is best understood as a severe, systemic allergic reaction, specifically a Type I hypersensitivity response, to a wide array of perioperative medications and substances, not limited to anesthetic agents. It is mediated by an exaggerated release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators from mast cells and basophils in genetically predisposed individuals. This results in a cascade of symptoms including generalized erythema or flushing, urticaria, angioedema (particularly concerning if it involves the airway), bronchospasm, hypotension from vasodilation, and a subsequent reactive tachycardia. The hyperthermia component is a secondary effect of the massive inflammatory response and increased metabolic rate, rather than a primary feature. Because it is an allergic phenomenon, prior exposure to the triggering agent is typically required to sensitize the immune system. Management mirrors that of anaphylaxis: immediate removal of the suspected trigger, securing the airway, administering epinephrine as the first-line drug, along with antihistamines (H1 and H2 blockers), corticosteroids, and intravenous fluids. Testing for susceptibility involves skin prick testing or specific IgE blood tests to identify the offending allergen, and prevention focuses on avoiding the identified agents. This contrasts with pharmacogenetic disorders, as the pathology here is immunologic, not related to muscle calcium homeostasis.
